title: FCL vs LCL — How to decide? | MB Fret Services
description: Choosing between FCL and LCL for your B2B sea freight and international moves: 13–15 m³ thresholds, safety, transit times and costs. A practical decision method with use cases on the France–Angola corridor.
hero_intro: Optimize total delivered cost, cargo safety and time-to-market for your containerised flows. A clear method to decide between FCL and LCL based on volume, deadlines and cargo sensitivity, for both companies and international movers.

p: FCL (Full Container Load) means you book a full container for your cargo. You control stuffing, sealing and routing, which generally improves security, traceability and lead-time reliability.

LCL (Less than Container Load) means your cargo is grouped with other shippers’ cargo. It introduces consolidation and deconsolidation steps, which may increase handling and transit time but keeps costs under control for smaller volumes.
Below roughly 13–15 m³, LCL is usually more competitive: you pay for the volume you actually use and avoid paying for empty container space.

Above that threshold, FCL quickly becomes attractive in cost per m³ and risk control (fewer handlings, less exposure). The exact switch point still depends on port pair, seasonality and carrier capacity.
For modest volumes (for example 1 to 5 pallets, only a few cubic metres), booking a full container is often sub‑optimal: you end up paying for a lot of empty space.

In such cases, LCL/groupage is usually the right fit: your pallets are consolidated with other shippers’ cargo, and you only pay for the volume you actually use, with a bit more handling and sometimes a slightly longer transit time.

As your volume approaches the 13–15 m³ range (or if cargo value/fragility is high), it becomes relevant to study a switch to a 20' FCL: lower cost per m³, fewer handlings, better control for international moves or sensitive goods.

ul: Volume/weight — CBM and gross weight: use a CBM calculator to size correctly.
Cargo value/sensitivity — FCL is often preferred for fragile or high-value goods.
Lead time — FCL is generally more direct; LCL implies consolidation steps.
Budget — compare FCL vs LCL on total delivered cost, not only on the ocean rate.
Internal capabilities — systems, partners and ability to manage bookings and deadlines.

ol: Compare a total delivered cost scenario FCL vs LCL for the relevant ports and season.
Arbitrate based on lead-time criticality and acceptable risk level.

sections.h2: Detailed costs: compare total delivered cost
ul: Sea freight + surcharges (BAF, CAF, PSS)
Origin/destination THC, BL/documentation and handling charges
Pre/post-carriage by road/rail and any storage/demurrage/detention
Ad valorem insurance, duties & taxes and admin/brokerage fees
p: The best option is not always the lowest ocean rate, but the setup that minimises total delivered cost for an acceptable risk level.

ul: LCL: more handling and transloading, which makes export-grade packaging essential (blocking, bracing, corner protection, clear labelling).
FCL: reduced mechanical stress thanks to dedicated container; focus on proper stuffing, lashing and ventilation if needed.
All modes: documentation consistency and proportionate insurance coverage are key to protecting cash flow and resolving any incident.
Small volume with flexible deadline: LCL with weekly consolidation and basic tracking.
Medium volume, sensitive goods: FCL 20' with professional packing and ad valorem insurance.
Large, recurring flows: FCL 40'/40'HC with fixed schedules and reserved slots to stabilise the supply chain.

p: LCL works well for parcels, baggage or test shipments; FCL quickly becomes the preferred option as soon as you combine international moves, B2B cargo and possibly vehicles or motorbikes within the same container, supported by ad valorem insurance.

A 20' container offers roughly 33 m³ of theoretical volume; a 40' around 67 m³. The effective usable volume depends on cargo type, weight constraints, stacking capability and any dangerous goods requirements. Export-grade packaging and careful palletisation reduce wasted space and the risk of damage.

sections.h2: 20' and 40' containers: usable volume and pallets
p: The figures below are indicative, to help you size your flows; actual loading always depends on cargo type, packaging and weight limitations.
ul: 20' dry container: roughly 33 m³ usable; up to about 11 Euro-pallets 80×120 cm or 10 pallets 100×120 cm on the floor; typical gross payload up to 18–20 tonnes.
40' dry container: roughly 67 m³ usable; up to about 23 pallets 80×120 cm or 20 pallets 100×120 cm on the floor; typical gross payload up to 26–28 tonnes.
40' High Cube (40'HC): slightly higher volume (≈ 76 m³), useful for light but bulky cargo.
Reefer, Open Top, Flat Rack and tank containers: available on a case-by-case basis for specific projects (temperature-controlled cargo, over-dimensioned pieces, bulk liquids, etc.).
Comparing only the ocean freight without including origin/destination and pre/post-carriage costs.
Ignoring seasonality and congestion on the route (peak season, holidays, strikes).
Underestimating the importance of export packaging and appropriate insurance for the cargo profile.
CBM/weight confirmed; cargo sensitivity assessed.
Ports and services selected; routing and cut-offs clearly understood.
FCL/LCL scenarios compared on total delivered cost, including pre/post-carriage and local charges.
Insurance and packaging documented and aligned with the chosen scenario.

faq.q: I’m a company: FCL or LCL for my pallets and B2B cargo on the France–Angola corridor?
faq.a: For B2B flows, we start by estimating your volume (in m³ or number of pallets), weight, regularity and cargo sensitivity. Below roughly 13–15 m³, LCL is usually more attractive: you pay only for the volume you really use, at the cost of a bit more handling. As soon as volumes grow or cargo is high-value/sensitive, 20' or 40' FCL often becomes more relevant in cost per m³, lead-time control and risk management.

faq.q: I’m moving to Angola: FCL or LCL for my personal effects and vehicle?
faq.a: For an international move, we assess your volume of personal effects (boxes, furniture, appliances, etc.) and whether a car or motorbike is included. For a small volume without a vehicle, LCL can be sufficient. As soon as you approach the 13–15 m³ range or combine personal effects and a vehicle in one shipment, a 20' or 40' FCL is usually the best option: one sealed container with packing, loading, ad valorem insurance and formalities integrated.

faq.q: Which volume threshold do you usually recommend to switch from LCL to FCL?
faq.a: As a rule of thumb, around 13–15 m³ is where FCL often becomes more attractive, both for B2B pallets and for moves. However, the actual threshold also depends on ports, seasonality (peak season, congestion) and cargo value/sensitivity: we always compare FCL/LCL scenarios on total delivered cost before recommending an option.
